https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Extinction Rebellion are criminals, says Priti Patel
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Activists in Extinction Rebellion are criminals who threaten the British way of life, Priti Patel said on Tuesday after the group’s blockade of printing presses.
In the harshest language used yet by any member of the government, the home secretary described the group as “so-called eco-crusaders turned criminals” who “disrupt our free society” with “guerrilla tactics”.
Speaking at the annual conference of the Police Superintendents’ Association, she vowed to crack down on the group, warning: “I refuse point-blank to allow that kind of anarchy on our streets.”
Ms Patel, whose parents set up a string of newsagents, challenged the police to use all the powers at their disposal “against those who threaten our freedoms”, describing the group as carrying out “a shameful attack on our way of life, our economy and the livelihoods of the hard-working majority”.
More than 100 environmental protesters from the group used vehicles and bamboo frames to block roads to the Newsprinters presses in Broxbourne in Hertfordshire and Knowsley in Merseyside on Friday night.
The presses publish titles including The Times, The Sun, The Daily Telegraph and the Daily Mail. Newsagents’ shelves were empty on Saturday morning, with delivery staff working round the clock to ensure that customers were still able to get hold of newspapers.
Millions of titles were wasted and pulped, and hundreds of additional journeys were made to get copies printed elsewhere, according to News UK, which is owned by News Corp, which owns the presses.
Reports have suggested that ministers are considering proposals to have the group classified as an organised crime group, which would make it an offence to assist it for gain.
Ms Patel said that further action against the group was the subject of a review of police powers .“Before we come up with new police powers, we have to effectively test the strength of existing police powers when it comes to policing these types of activities we saw at the weekend, which are completely unacceptable and disruptive to society and our economy and to people working in a particular sector,” she said.
“I just think it’s wrong, completely wrong. We saw an organisation deploy extreme tactics, guerrilla tactics, to bring very significant disruption. [They] undermined a functioning society, not just with getting newspapers out, but attacking people’s jobs and livelihoods, attacking critical parts of our economy.”
Ms Patel refuted the group’s claims to have been carrying out peaceful protest. She said: “These are tactics that are deployed to cause maximum damage to society — blocking of roads, for example. Last week we saw ambulances and blue lights not even being able to get through to hospitals. . . threatening people’s lives in addition to the economic wellbeing of our society at a time when actually we’re trying to get society up and running all over again.”
Paul Griffiths, president of the Police Superintendents’ Association, said: “Policing peaceful protest is a really important part of our democracy. But actually, when it starts to impede economically, we do need the powers to deal with that situation.”
Further details emerged on Tuesday surrounding some of those who have been charged with obstructing a public highway following the protest at the printing presses.
Caspar Hughes, 49, the boss of a cycling courier company, Mandy Leathers, 53, who has previously set up petitions calling for the banning of fur, and Hamish Haynes, 46, who was previously cleared of obstructing a highway during an anti-fracking protest at a Cuadrilla test site in Lancashire, were among 77 people charged.
The Labour MP Dawn Butler reignited a debate about the party’s position on Extinction Rebellion and its blockade of printing presses. She had deleted a tweet praising the protest, but said she had done so accidentally and denied acting under pressure from the party leadership.
She told BBC’s Politics Live: “I support Extinction Rebellion, not everything they do, but at the end of the day they were making a point and a statement. We have a right to protest.”
Ms Butler, who is MP for Brent Central, criticised discussion on whether to reclassify Extinction Rebellion as an organised crime group, saying: “We have a right to free protest in this country and that shouldn’t be interfered with, as implied by the government yesterday.”
Separately, it has been revealed that Zion Lights, 35, a mother-of-two from Exeter who has appeared as a “chief spokesperson” for Extinction Rebellion, has left the organisation and is now a campaigner for nuclear energy, supporting the proposed Sizewell C power station in Suffolk.
Activists and business people . . . protesters facing court
The boss of a cycling courier company, an anti-fur campaigner and an astrophysics student were among those arrested over the Extinction Rebellion protests at Newsprinters sites on Friday.
Cycling company boss Caspar Hughes, from Exeter, runs events for a cycling courier business that has worked with Adidas and the BBC. He told his local paper Devon Live that “society is heading for cultural collapse within decades”. In June he was involved in a protest in which traffic cones were laid out to reinforce a cycle lane in Exeter.
Anti-fur protester Mandy Leathers, 53, from Bury St Edmunds in Suffolk, has set up a petition calling for the wearing of fur to be banned after seeing it on sale in a local market. Last year an appeal on Justgiving raised £350 to buy her a new bike after hers was confiscated by police at a protest. It said: “As Mandy dedicates so much time to her voluntary activism work she has low earnings.”
Astrophysics student Janna Goldstein, 26, from Birmingham, is completing a PhD in astrophysics at Birmingham University. She wrote on her Linkedin profile: “It is important to me to have a positive impact on the world, and I hope to find an employer who values equality and sustainability, for example.”
Student gardener Lucy Walsh, 24, from York, is a vegan who founded York University’s gardening society.
Film-maker Harrison Radcliffe, 21, from Leeds, worked for Oldham council before quitting to become a “full-time activist”. He has been involved in several protests, including gluing himself to a Barclays bank.
Author Rebeccah Plenderleith, 50, from Berkhamsted in Hertfordshire is author of a “saucy” guide to love.
Anti-fracker Hamish Haynes, 46, from Stalybridge in Greater Manchester, was one of ten Greenpeace activists who were cleared of obstructing a highway after protesting at Cuadrilla's shale gas test site at Little Plumpton, Lancashire, in 2017. District judge Jeff Brailsford found they had been sitting calmly and peacefully. He said the defendants held “genuine beliefs and are entitled to express those beliefs”.
Town councillor Robert Mackenzie, a town councillor from Long Stratton, near Norwich, owns a £600,000 farmhouse with a long drive where he parks his silver Mazda MX-5 sports car.
Company director Gail Thomas, 51, from Stamford, Lincolnshire, is a director of several companies, including Gems Lingerie, which makes “comfortable knickers”. She is also the founder and chief executive of a virtual PA business, and director of a business administration company and a management consultancy.
Recruitment consultant Mark Fletcher, 45, is a director of a recruitment firm called Brightstar in Norwich. He says on his company website: “When I’m not working I'm either dreaming about the next cool or unusual guitar I'd like to add to my collection or embarrassing myself in front of my kids at the skate park!”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/david-c.title: David Cameron left squirming over Sasha Swire’s tales of indecorum
https://www.thetimes.com/article/david-c.text:
David Cameron has revealed he was left red-faced by the diaries of a Tory MP’s wife that detail his personal feuds, drinking and sex jokes, admitting: “It’s kind of embarrassing.”
The former prime minister insisted that he could not recall an incident described by Sasha Swire, wife of the MP Sir Hugo Swire, in which he allegedly joked that her perfume made him want to push her “into the bushes and give you one”.
But in an interview with Times Radio to be broadcast today — in which he also called for Jeremy Hunt to return to frontline politics — he had his head in his hands as he said that the betrayal by longstanding friends was not what you wanted “splashed all over the place”.
Lady Swire’s memoir, serialised in The Times, has sent shock waves through the Cameron clique, describing “Dave”, his wife, Samantha, and colleagues including George Osborne, Michael Gove and Boris Johnson in their most private moments.
The Secret Diary of an MP’s Wife recounts a number of holidays and dinners and even the night Mr Cameron resigned as prime minister after the Brexit referendum in June 2016.
In his first public remarks on the book, Mr Cameron said: “Look. Of course, it’s kind of . . . it’s embarrassing when you have things you say in private and do in private, sort of splashed all over the place, and of course you’d rather that didn’t happen.
“I suppose the truth is that if you want respect for your privacy and people not questioning your character and private life and all the rest of it, then politics probably isn’t the career for you.”
Lady Swire claims that Mr Cameron insisted she go behind him on a coastal walk because “the scent you are wearing is affecting my pheromones. It makes me want to grab you and push you into the bushes and give you one.”
Mr Cameron said: “I don’t recall that conversation . . . if someone wrote down all your banter in private over the years, there probably might be a few bits and pieces that weren’t very flattering.”
In the interview, Mr Cameron also said that Mr Johnson should not fear “tall poppies” in his cabinet and said he hoped Mr Hunt’s talent would not be “lost to politics for ever”.
Amid widespread criticism of the calibre of the present cabinet, the former prime minister said it was good to have “big beasts” in the top team.
Mr Cameron warned that the Conservatives risked appearing less “socially inclusive and progressive” in pursuit of Brexit. He also revealed that he spent lockdown working in a food bank and that his daughter, Nancy, 16, is an environmental activist and wants him to cut down on meat.
The rivalry between Mr Cameron and Mr Johnson, both Old Etonians, dates back years and they fell out dramatically after Mr Johnson supported Leave in the 2016 referendum.
Most prominent supporters of Mr Cameron have since left the cabinet and in many cases parliament. Mr Hunt, who was defeated by Mr Johnson for the Tory leadership last year, lost his job as foreign secretary and is chairman of the health select committee.
Mr Cameron said Britain would be better served with a more heavyweight cabinet. In his first major interview publicising the paperback edition of his memoirs, For The Record, he said: “My approach was . . . I didn’t fear the tall poppies”, pointing to veterans including Lord Clarke of Nottingham, Lord Hague of Richmond, Sir George Young and Sir Iain Duncan Smith who served in his early cabinets.
He declined to confirm whether he voted for Mr Hunt to be leader, but, pressed on whether he thought his friend should be back in the cabinet, said: “Jeremy is hugely capable. I hope his talent isn’t lost to politics for ever.”
Mr Cameron also took a swipe at Dominic Cummings, Mr Johnson’s chief adviser, with whom he clashed when Mr Cummings worked for Mr Gove. “Well I did sack him twice but he kept coming back. We didn’t necessarily hit it off but he’s a man of great, I mean he’s very clever, he is very able.
“Perhaps if he’s your right-hand man and you’re the prime minister that’s the best place for him. It’s just, he wasn’t my right-hand man, he was someone else’s, and it was no end of trouble.”
Mr Cameron also suggested that he would have taken a more hands-on approach in the pandemic, following criticism that Mr Johnson missed five Cobra meetings as the crisis began.
As prime minister he set up the Threats, Hazards, Resilience and Contingencies committee which he says put the threat of a pandemic “on the radar”, but conceded that it was too focused on a flu outbreak. He rejected the idea that years of austerity and a failure to reform social care contributed to the high death toll in care homes.
Mr Cameron, who was close to President Obama, did not reserve his criticism for domestic issues. He said that “Trump drives everyone mad, he certainly drives me mad”. Asked which candidate for the presidency would be best for Britain, he added: “If you want to see global action on climate change, if you want to see action to continue to deal with the scourge of global poverty, if you want to see a promotion of trade and anti-protectionism, I mean it’s hard to argue that Donald Trump is good for those things.”
In a new foreword to his memoir, Mr Cameron acknowledges that his effort to embrace China while in office may have failed, asking: “Was that misguided, or even counterproductive?”
Having begun his leadership of the Tories in 2005 by hugging a huskie and installing a wind turbine on his London home, Mr Cameron’s green campaigning has been taken up by his daughter Nancy. “She . . . went on one of the big marches, and I was applauding her for caring about it and for marching but sort of my worry is that Extinction Rebellion are asking the impossible.”
During the lockdown his wife, Samantha, had been “battling to save” her fashion business, while he homeschooled their three children. “I worked for the Chipping Norton Food Bank, actually, one or two days a week, which was great to do something to help people who were really isolated.”
Listen to Matt Chorley’s interview with David Cameron on Times Radio from 10am.

image.caption: David Cameron said Sasha Swire’s memoir was not the sort of thing you wanted “splashed all over the place”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Jail has no vegan meals, complains eco-activist Roger Hallam
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
The co-founder of Extinction Rebellion complained about living in a cockroach-infested cell with inadequate vegan food as he was released on bail to face trial for allegedly plotting to vandalise trades union properties.
Roger Hallam, 54, was arrested last month and remanded in custody amid claims a Green Party member “infiltrated” a meeting and passed details to police of an alleged plot to throw paint over the buildings of four unions.
Mr Hallam, a former organic farmer and sociologist who helped set up the pressure group in 2018, was arrested alongside four others who have all worked with Extinction Rebellion.
Mr Hallam appeared yesterday via videolink at Wood Green crown court where he denied a charge of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.
Last year he was disowned by the German branch of Extinction Rebellion for insisting there was nothing “unique” about the Holocaust and went on to withdraw from his formal positions within the UK group. He then set up the Beyond Politics political party, which is part of the Burning Pink network.
Mr Hallam, who was arrested at his home in Putney, southwest London, and Diana Warner, a former GP from Bristol, went on hunger strike while on remand.
The court was told that Mr Hallam was being held in poor conditions, which included the presence of cockroaches. Burning Pink said after his release that “in prison, [Mr] Hallam shared his cell with cockroaches and mice. He was denied a desk and it took the guards a week before they could provide him with a pillow.
“For five days he was only allowed out of his cell for 40 minutes, he noticed more fighting compared to his previous time in prison and was denied any vegan or vegetarian food options that constitute a balanced meal.”
Burning Pink (Beyond Politics) said that Mr Hallam “emerged from prison keen to make peace with [the individual whose allegations to police are thought to have led to his arrest and that of Ms Warner], inviting him to speak with him so he could understand their actions”.
Ferhat Ulusu, 42, a freelance photographer of east London; Holly Brentnall, 29, of north London and Steven Nunn, 56, an Anglican priest from Telford, were arrested and charged alongside Mr Hallam and Ms Warner.
Ms Warner and Mr Ulusu also denied the charge. They and Mr Hallam are due to appear again at Wood Green crown court on November 27. Ms Brentnall and Mr Nunn have not entered pleas and are due to appear again at Wood Green on November 6.
Extinction Rebellion said that Ms Brentnall, also known as Blyth, a journalist, Mr Ulusu, Mr Nunn and Ms Warner had worked with the group.

image.caption: Roger Hallam helped set up Extinction Rebellion two years ago but has now left the group

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Inspiring? Exciting? No, just Gavin the gormless
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Citizens, we can relax. It’s going to be all right now: MPs are back at Westminster. And who, seeing the education secretary Gavin Williamson at the despatch box, could doubt the quality of our helms-people?
Gormless Gavin was giving a statement on the A-level results and on the reopening of schools. Children were going to be “inspired by their teachers”, he said in that hollow, nasal tone that strips the word “inspire” of all its potential. He stood with shoulders hunched, his whole political personality somehow frozen, as if expecting to be clanged over the head by a frying pan at any moment.
Given that the MPs behind him included three recent cabinet ministers (Alun Cairns, Damian Hinds and the sulphurously, snortingly snooty Caroline Nokes), you could hardly blame him. All three might have been forgiven for thinking “I’d do better than that!”
Personally, I loved the mournful way Mr Williamson announced that the head of Ofqual, Sally Collier, had come to her own decision that “the next stage of the exam results awarding process would be better overseen by someone else”. Translation: we sacked her for being even more useless than me! Collier or Williamson: close call.
After the exams balls-up, one of them had to be placed in the trebuchet harness and sent hurtling into the distant yonder. Mr Williamson went on to say that children would now “be able to embark on the next exciting stage of their lives”. That “exciting” was inspired.
On Parliament Square, Extinction Rebellion youngsters were banging drums and being blasted by Muslim prayers, Jewish chants and hippy meditation about the “lineage of wisdom”. Turnout was light. Maybe some of their colleagues were protesting from home. “Look around you with eyes of love,” bawled a woman whose posh accent was being amplified so loudly, it outdid the jungle drums. A guitarist later shouted the F-word and had to apologise, saying “I know I shouldn’t swear in front of the children who are here”.
The eyes-of-love message was, alas, lost on Ms Nokes. On a lunchtime telly show she hungrily put the boot into the proposed involvement at our Board of Trade of a former Australian prime minister, Tony Abbott. Ms Nokes accused Mr Abbott of all manner of anti-equalities sins. He is also pro-Brexit and right-wing, which may be the real problem. Ms Nokes is not really either of those. The thought of hiring him was “such a bad idea, I’m not sure I can come up with words for how awful it is,” she said with immense grandeur.
Mr Abbott appeared a short while later at a virtual meeting of the foreign affairs select committee. He was enjoying the political argy-bargy enormously. He called it “banter” and kept chuckling, which only made the lefties even crosser. Labour’s Claudia Webbe (Leicester E), from her shiny kitchen, claimed that Mr Abbott once said men were “by physiology or temper more adapted than women to exercise authority”. How, she wondered, would he like taking instructions from the trade secretary Liz Truss?
Mr Abbott laughed and said he did not recall ever saying such a thing. As far as his involvement with the Board of Trade went, nothing was yet official and he was reluctant to go into details. Chris Bryant (Lab, Rhondda) wondered if he had answered a job advert in The Guardian. “I don’t normally read The Guardian,” confessed Mr Abbott, with another Aussie grin. “But I’m sure it’s a wonderful newspaper.”
Back in the Commons we heard, at terrible length, from the health secretary, Matt Hancock — minus his Union Jack mask, thank goodness. He was back in military mode, repeatedly talking about “boots on the ground” and talking of coronavirus as “the enemy”. The next stage of the war will be an “All In, All Together” advertising campaign to boost national unity. I’m all in.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: The BBC’s smug lefties won’t be laughing now
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
One grey, exhausted patriarch bows out, with a final defiant expression of hope for the BBC. Tomorrow a younger one sets out his stall as director-general. Do we hold our breath, or glumly expect the usual stuff about attracting youth, fostering diversity, being an international voice and rationalising management (probably by hiring consultants and inventing yet more senior posts)? We’ve heard it all before. But Middle England, despite our media snarking, basically still loves the BBC. Sometimes exasperated by news bias, national hearts hold grateful memories all the way from Life with the Lyons to Line of Duty.
Lately there was genuine appreciation of the treats the corporation offered during lockdown. There is even some sympathy for its struggles in the age of streaming and subscription, as it pants on like a stout old dog with its fringe in its eyes, teased by nimble yapping pups. We middling-majority hope that Tim Davie loves it too, but enough to shake it by the scruff of the neck, get the clippers out and take the old mutt for a brisk run down some new tracks.
An interesting leak says the new boss is concerned at the perception that its radio and TV comedy and satire tend to be one-sided: not only biased against Tories, Brexit and Donald Trump but with an unchallenged metropolitan sensibility. MPs have complained, as has the culture secretary and, two years back, its own Andrew Neil blasting the “self-adulatory unchallenged left-wing propaganda” and “contrived ideological commentary” of news-based comedy panels. Face it, even the leftiest of us know exactly what he means. Even when we quite like some of the jokes.
It is a brave DG who takes on something as necessarily frothy as comedy, but perhaps Mr Davie feels up to it. It’s a tough time to do it, after ten years of Conservative power and at least four more to come. Some government measures have caused disproportionate suffering to the economically weakest, others brought on a miserably chaotic Brexit process. Now, in an unprecedented pandemic, it makes errors which if we’re honest (rather than seizing them as comedy gold), any government might make. Our prime minister generously offers hilarious material, from his locks to his Latinisms, and the president of the US regularly delivers a level of callous buffoonery which few comic writers apart from absurdist Alfred Jarry could better. Given all this, is there any wonder that mainstream comedy unthinkingly leans left?
The BBC is rightly a great patron of the genre, so that is where a lot of it ends up. But that also means that the BBC is precisely the place where it should be more intelligently managed and recruited. It isn’t; its comedy scouts cling to a few high-paid stars and spend too little time scoping fringe clubs. And a left-wing bias is easiest to find. Comedians are performers who hunger to be loved, so it helps to sound like the nice guy, and also to seem young and fresh. So even if in reality you are highly paid, comfortable, and well into middle age and middle class, it helps to pose as being on the side of the underdog, the poor, the outsider, the different.
Laughter also likes vituperation and scorn. So they hit out and, being the nice guy, ostentatiously “punch upward” even if the targets are so hackneyed it’s like shooting fish in a barrel. Attacking power makes even the most banal joker in a safe society feel like a gallant ally of the courageous samizdat comedians and cartoonists in Russia, China or Iran. But it doesn’t necessarily make them any good.
Comedy thinks it’s the new rock’n’roll, but many of its practitioners are hardly even Mantovani. Seriously, when did you last hear a truly funny, original Trump or Boris joke? When did the unspeakably smug Nish Kumar, The Now Show, or any of the woke young gunslingers on panel shows make you see something afresh and giggle half-guiltily? When were you last amusedly shocked on The News Quiz on Radio 4, in the way Alan Coren or Linda Smith achieved quite regularly with (certainly in Alan’s case) a willingness to laugh at both left and right?
The BBC tries to introduce moderate-right journalists into news quizzes, but the prevailing tone of its shows is unmistakable and boringly sameish. Targets could be wider, funnier, cheekier about all edges of society. Forget the boring Trump or Matt Hancock gags and tilt, for example, at the affronted fury of people who went abroad when it was already likely that quarantine rules could change, or at the sillier pretensions of demonstrators — BLM and Extinction Rebellion as well as David Icke-style crazies. Annoy and amuse more kinds of people.
Broadcast comedy matters. It sweetens life, from Father Ted to Friday Night Dinner. The BBC nurtured Victoria Wood once, and Jack Dee’s cruelly brilliant satire on his own profession in Lead Balloon (though it failed to grab his even funnier, punching up-down-and-sideways show about miserable ruralites, Bad Move). On iPlayer these tedious months I was held together by the retro absurdities of I’m Sorry I Haven’t a Clue and Just A Minute, found old Ab Fabs and Yes Ministers on streaming services and the pleasingly un-woke targets of Armstrong and Miller on YouTube. None of these joys, even Yes Minister, felt as gloweringly and fruitlessly political as the shows Mr Davie is reputed to have in his sights. Come on Tim!
Alice Thomson is away

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Squat mother in court over Extinction Rebellion blockade
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
A woman with nine children appeared in court yesterday with 50 others accused of being involved in an Extinction Rebellion blockade of printing presses.
Natalie Bracht, 45, appeared at Luton magistrates’ court via video link from Stevenage police station on one charge of obstruction of the highway. The court was told that she had been offered legal representation but turned it down.
She is among 51 people who have been charged with obstruction of the highway after the protest in Hertfordshire on Friday night. Extinction Rebellion targeted the Newsprinters print works, which produces newspapers including The Times, The Sun, The Daily Telegraph and the Daily Mail.
Ms Bracht initially failed to respond to questions about her name and personal details and did not provide an address to the court. She was later charged with obstructing a police officer. Judge Sally Fudge entered a plea of not guilty on her behalf.
Ms Bracht later gave her address as a squat in a garden in Sipson, near Heathrow airport. “It’s not a building, it’s a squat place and there are a number of people living there,” she said.
She was released on conditional bail to appear at St Albans magistrates’ court along with 50 other suspects and ordered not to go within 100 metres of the boundary of any Newsprinters premises. She was also told not to enter Hertfordshire before November 14 and not to attend any protest linked to Extinction Rebellion.
Yesterday, a charity defended press freedom after it emerged that a senior executive had been charged following the protest. Cleodie Rickard, 24, a Cambridge graduate, works in the policy and public affairs executive at the Charities Aid Foundation.
The charity, which describes itself as a “bank and champion” for donors, companies and charities, would not confirm Ms Rickard’s employment status, but said: “Part of our promotion of civil society is respect for a free press. We are strong advocates for a civil society and a pillar of that is a free press.”
It also emerged last night that a lawyer who is leading Extinction Rebellion’s legal defence was previously deputy director of the government’s organised crime agency. Tim Crosland was head of cyber, prevention and information law at the Serious Organised Crime Agency (Soca) which was merged into the National Crime Agency. He has questioned the government’s attempts to designate Extinction Rebellion as an organised crime group.
He told The Daily Telegraph: “The thing we are focused on at the moment is the threat from Boris Johnson to classify Extinction Rebellion as an organised crime group. I used to work for Soca, and I was involved in the drafting of some of this [legislation].
“The idea this applies to ordinary people like grandmothers and nurses is quite a stretch . . . They must also show a motive of gain. Organised criminals are about making a profit. That is the one thing you really couldn’t say about a direct action movement protesting for a wider cause. It is an extraordinary thing for the government to suggest that people taking direct action in the manner of suffragettes should be treated as organised criminals.”
Kit Malthouse, the Home Office minister in charge of policing, has said that police would look at what lessons needed to be learnt after it took Hertfordshire police 12 hours to clear the scene.
Cleodie RickardA policy and public affairs executive at the Charities Aid Foundation, Cleodie Rickard, 24, has a history of speaking out on moral issues.
She was one of ten Cambridge students who accused a vice-master of sexual misconduct, waiving her right to anonymity. Dr Peter Hutchinson was said to have offered to give one student a “big kiss” on her birthday, made comments about their clothing and asked students if they would “sleep [their] way to the top”. Dr Hutchinson was banned from Trinity Hall and from contacting students but was readmitted less than two years later. He has said he “deeply regretted” making the comments.
Ms Rickard, from London, speaks four foreign languages and graduated with a first-class degree in Arabic and Middle Eastern Studies. She was briefly held by Israeli security officers while in the Palestinian territories for her course in 2017. She has worked for Save the Children UK and has volunteered at a Calais refugee camp.
Steve ToozeA self-declared “Corbyn-supporting leftie”, Steve Tooze declared that he had worked “for every one of these newspapers in the last 25 years” at the Broxbourne print works blockade on Friday.
Indeed, the 56-year-old Londoner’s byline has appeared in newspapers including the now-defunct News of the World, the Daily Mirror, the Daily Mail, the Sunday Mail, The Sunday Telegraph and The Mail on Sunday.
Now a consultant at the “global trend analyst Stylus”, he has worked with organisations including the BBC, Nissan and Amazon, who have “benefited from his talent for discovering what they most need to know about the evolving trend landscape”, according to the Stylus website.
A technology enthusiast, he has commented on how Amazon will make long-haul travel easier and quicker. “From Alexa finding our flights and checking the weather at our destination to bluetooth locators and smart fingerprint locks for our luggage, there is a high-tech gadget to make every element of our summer holiday easier,” he said.
He was previously head of global insights at the agency the Future Laboratory, helping to produce reports into matters such as artificial intelligence in British gardens, and future job roles.
These included, he said, a “virtual habitat designer” who would ask: “What is it exactly about sitting under a tree in real life that’s pleasurable? How can we replicate that in the virtual world?”
He now says “we need media who tell the truth about the climate crisis”.
William FarbrotherIn March 2017, when William Farbrother was working as a researcher for the Department for Work and Pensions in London, Khalid Masood drove a car over Westminster Bridge, near the Houses of Parliament, killing five, including PC Keith Palmer.
Mr Farbrother wrote on his Facebook page at the time: “I’m fine, thanks for asking . . . it’s becoming increasingly clear this was an exceptionally vicious act, but [to be honest], I’m still far more bothered about London’s NO2 crisis than terrorism.”
Mr Farbrother says on his LinkedIn page that he has been a senior researcher on the social security advisory committee since September 2016. He comes from York, where his parents run a bed and breakfast, but now lives in Walthamstow, east London.
His father, John Farbrother, told The Times: “When we’ve got three to four helicopters hovering over London, and thousands of police, all on overtime, at protests during lockdown, and none of this gets covered on the main broadcasters or in the national media, then you wonder why they take action outside the presses?
“I support the movement’s [Extinction Rebellion] ambitions. I think we all should, because it’s an absolutely critical issue that we’ve got to get a hold of as a government policy.”
The Department for Work and Pensions declined to comment. All three of those profiled have been charged with obstruction of the highway.

image.caption: Cleodie Rickard has a first-class Cambridge degree in Arabic, Steve Tooze has written on the future of long-haul travel and William Farbrother is a civil servant
Natalie Bracht lives in a squat near Heathrow and turned down legal representation when she appeared before magistrates yesterday

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.title: Trouble on the line as Extinction Rebellion protesters fight HS2
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.text:
For a few weeks in 1996-97, it seemed that Daniel Hooper was the most famous man in England. Swampy, as he was known, spent seven days in tunnels excavated under the path of the enlarging A30 near Exeter. The A30 protest ultimately failed, but its like has been replicated several times since then and “Swampy” has become a catch-all for any environmental activist taking to the earth or the trees. It is a term that is being heard once again.
Having finally gained the backing of the prime minister just before the pandemic began, construction work started this month on Europe’s largest infrastructure project. The first phase of the HS2 rail line snaking through the Chilterns and Shakespeare country is due to deliver high-speed train services between Birmingham and London by the start of the next decade.
Having lost the economic, environmental and societal debates on the project, dissenters are left with one last arrow to unleash: direct action. An unlikely alliance of environmentalists and ecowarriors, the Swampies de nos jours, apparently funded by a well-to-do tendency of not-in-my-back-yarders in the Home Counties and Tory shire seats along the line’s path, have become active in recent months.
From hundreds of demonstraters in the Colne Valley next to Mr Johnson’s west London constituency, which the line crosses, direct action has spread north. There have been flashpoints at Great Missenden in Buckinghamshire, as activists seek to protect woodland beloved of Roald Dahl, the author, and further north in the county at the Calvert Jubilee nature reserve. This week protests have broken out in Warwickshire at Cubbington Woods, near Leamington Spa.
With the recent success of action by Extinction Rebellion to prevent the distribution of newspapers such as The Times last week, the environmental movement has become emboldened, even if the arguments against HS2 have become diffuse.
In addition to ecological destruction, campaigners argue against the carbon impact of the line, even if few doubt that rail is preferable to road and that HS2, as a north-south relief railway, will displace freight from motorways on to the west coast main line, which HS2 is designed to decongest. Some have revisited the old saw that this is a Conservative project designed to aid the party’s business chums, ignoring the fact that it was launched by Gordon Brown’s Labour government. More recent is the slogan “NHS not HS2” — people are more interested in their taxes being spent on fighting the pandemic.
The flare-ups at Cubbington are becoming a regular event, with trespassers blocking vehicles and being ejected by security guards or the police on a near-daily basis. A protest camp has been cleared, but demonstrators have decamped to Crackley Wood, where the line bends south of Coventry between the country town of Kenilworth and the sprawling University of Warwick campus.
There, activists have set up between 30 and 40 tents on a meadow abutting the line with the permission of a landowner. From there, they make the eight-mile daily commute to Cubbington in battered vans.
Protesters at Cubbington, including women, claim that they have been manhandled by HS2 operatives. “We are back in court again,” one said this week. “Aggravated trespass. Again.”
HS2 says that the protests are a safety risk, wasting public money — £16 million has been spent on security at the last count — and stretching police resources. The company cites the ruling of the judge in a legal challenge that the works have been authorised by Westminster and that “there is a strong public interest in ensuring that activities sanctioned by parliament are not stopped by individuals because they do not personally agree with them”.
HS2 said: “All leading environmental organisations agree that climate change is the biggest threat to wildlife and habitats in the UK. HS2 will provide a cleaner, greener way to travel.”
Contractors say that they have no idea how serious the incursions might become. Dealing with demonstrators in woodlands is not, they contend, as big an issue as it will be when, as is predicted, demonstrators target more strategic locations around the tunnels to be cut under the Chilterns or the complex construction work nearer Birmingham, where HS2 crosses roads, canals and existing railway lines.
Cubbington and Crackley are part of the ancient Forest of Arden eulogised by Shakespeare. Post-industrialisation, the forest no longer exists. It is why these ancient outcrops of beech, birch and oak matter to people.
Protesters have occupied diggers and claim that their action has been legitimised by the prime minister himself. “What did Boris say about the third runway [at Heathrow]? That he’d lie down in front of the bulldozers?” one said.
But are the protesters in for the long haul? “My wife asked me that the other day,” said Jim, a man in his fifties, who claimed to have been at the camp since March. “But [gesturing towards the path cleared by the bulldozers through the woods] that’s a scar on the countryside. What else are we supposed to do?”
